problem: Language-conditioned navigation methods (VLN) need large datasets of trajectories annotated with instructions, often simulated and hard to build for unstructured outdoor settings. Self-supervised goal-conditioned navigation policies scale to real robots from unlabeled data, but users can only specify goals as images or GPS locations.
motivation: Pre-trained LLMs and vision-language models generalize well and already exist off the shelf. Self-supervised navigation models such as ViNG can build topological maps and drive robustly in the real world. The paper observes that chaining these independently trained models through a probabilistic planning objective could give a natural-language interface to a real robot with no language-annotated robot data and no fine-tuning.
key_idea: Compose three frozen pre-trained models: GPT-3 extracts an ordered list of landmarks from the instruction, CLIP scores every topological-graph node against every landmark, and ViNG supplies edge distances and low-level control. A Dijkstra-style dynamic program then finds the walk that jointly maximizes landmark likelihood and traversability.
insight: Neither grounding alone nor distance alone is enough; the joint objective is what makes the system work. Ablating the traversability term leaves a Max Likelihood planner that is much worse: planning success falls from 0.9/0.8 to 0.6/0.2 (EnvSmall/EnvLarge) and planning efficiency from 0.80/0.99 to 0.69/0.17. The distance term acts as a soft spatial prior that also filters CLIP false positives, e.g. variable-binding errors such as a blue truck being retrieved for 'blue dumpster'. Replacing the learned navigation model with GPS distances plus a straight-line controller drops net success from 0.8 to 0.23 and raises disengagements from 0.1 to 0.75, so learned traversability is essential in cluttered outdoor scenes. The component studies point to visual grounding as the bottleneck: CLIP detects landmarks at 0.87 (vs ViLD 0.38, Faster-RCNN 0.07), and every full-system failure traced back to CLIP missing 'hard' landmarks.
method: Topological graph via ViNG: nodes are images plus GPS from a manually driven prior traversal. Edges are added when timestamps are within ε (1 s), or when ViNG's learned temporal distance is below τ=80 steps (~20 m) AND GPS distance is below η=100 m (to avoid wormholes). Edge weight is the ViNG distance; a transitive reduction then prunes redundant edges.

LLM landmark parsing: GPT-3 (temperature 0) with a 3-example in-context prompt turns a free-form instruction into an ordered list of textual landmarks, handling re-orderings such as 'after you pass X'.
VLM grounding: CLIP scores each node image against the caption 'This is a photo of a [landmark]'. A softmax over all nodes gives P(v|ℓ).

Probabilistic objective: success likelihood = ∏γ^{D(v_j,v_{j+1})} (discounted traversability from ViNG distances) × max over monotone landmark-to-node assignments of ∏P(v_{t_i}|ℓ_i). This is equivalent to maximizing R = ΣCLIP(v_{t_i},ℓ_i) − α·ΣD with α=−log γ.
Graph search: dynamic programming Q(i,v) = max(Q(i−1,v)+CLIP(v,ℓ_i), max_w Q(i,w)−α·D(v,w)), computed with a Dijkstra-like pass for each landmark index, followed by backtracking from argmax Q(n,·).
Execution: ViNG's goal-conditioned policy drives the Clearpath Jackal along the walk's subgoal images on board, using only the forward RGB camera and GPS.

setting.backbone: GPT-3 (frozen, OpenAI API) + CLIP ViT (frozen) + ViNG goal-conditioned navigation model (pre-trained, frozen)
setting.model_size: not stated (GPT-3 API model unspecified; CLIP ViT variant unspecified)
setting.training_data: none for this system (training-free composition). ViNG is pre-trained in prior work on self-supervised, unlabeled robot trajectories via hindsight relabeling; no language-annotated robot data.
setting.observation: front-facing RGB (170° FOV) + unfiltered GPS for control; the graph is built from images + GPS + timestamps of a prior traversal
setting.action_space: subgoal nodes of a topological graph, executed by ViNG's low-level control policy
setting.privileged: pre-exploration: a manually driven traversal of each environment (images + GPS) is used to build the topological graph before instructions are given; GPS localization

numbers_note: Custom real-world evaluation only: 20 instructions over more than 6 km in total. Values are printed as fractions (0.8 → 80). SR here is the paper's 'Net Success'. Efficiency is averaged over successful runs only. Diseng is the average number of interventions per run, not a percentage. The text says LM-Nav follows instructions in '85% of the experiments' with 'an average of 1 intervention per 6.4km', whereas Table 1 shows Net Success 0.8 in both environments; the numbers above follow the table. Component-level evaluations are omitted from the numbers list because they are not navigation benchmarks: landmark extraction success (GPT-3 1.0 on the 20 prompts) and CLIP-ViT detection rate (0.87 on 100 images / 30 landmarks, top-3).
results: On a Clearpath Jackal in outdoor suburban environments, LM-Nav reached 0.8 net success in both EnvSmall-10 and EnvLarge-10, with efficiency 0.96/0.89 and 0.1/0 disengagements, on routes of hundreds of meters (goals up to 800 m away). It clearly beats the GPS-Nav ablation, which uses straight-line control without ViNG: 0.23 net success and 0.75 disengagements on EnvSmall-10. It also beats a Max Likelihood planner, which reaches only 0.2 planning success and 0.17 planning efficiency on EnvLarge-10 (vs 0.8 and 0.99). In the component studies, GPT-3 (1.0) outperforms GPT-J-6B, GPT-NeoX-20B, fairseq and spaCy noun chunks for landmark extraction, and CLIP (0.87) outperforms ViLD and Faster-RCNN for grounding.
limitations: Only landmarks are used: verbs and other nuanced commands (e.g., 'go straight for three blocks', 'drive slowly') are ignored.
Requires a prior traversal of the environment to build the topological graph, and relies on GPS. The ViNG model is specific to outdoor navigation with the Jackal robot.

Grounding with CLIP fails on 'hard' landmarks (fire hydrant, cement mixer) and in poor lighting, and was the source of all full-system failures. The evaluation is small (20 instructions) and uses a custom real-world setup with no standard benchmark.
